titre: Mary Anning Found the Fossils, Others Signed the Papers
accroche: She discovered the first complete ichthyosaur, plesiosaur and pterosaur in Great Britain, without ever being able to sign a scientific paper.
contenu_vulgarise:
At Lyme Regis, on the Dorset coast, the Lias cliffs collapse after every winter storm and release fossils nearly 200 million years old. This is where Mary Anning, the daughter of a cabinetmaker who died riddled with debts, learns from childhood the trade of “curiosity seeker”: selling visitors what the sea uncovers. In the fall of 1811, her brother Joseph spots a skull; it is only in November 1812 that she uncovers the rest of a marine skeleton more than five meters long, the first ichthyosaur ever identified as such. In December 1823, it is she who unearths the first complete plesiosaur skeleton; in 1828, the first British pterosaur, a Dimorphodon. Three groups of extinct animals, later popularized in 19th-century geology textbooks, pass first through her hands.

## A Signature That Is Never Hers

Anning sells her finds to wealthy collectors, clergymen, amateur geologists, members of the Geological Society of London, who then describe them in scholarly papers. The name that appears on the article is that of the buyer, not that of the woman who spent weeks uncovering, cleaning and often correctly identifying the specimen. The Geological Society, in any case, would not have let her sign: founded in 1807, it admits women as *Fellows* only from May 21, 1919. Anning dies in 1847, seventy-two years too early. Without fortune, without status, without a degree, she remains all her life a supplier who is cited in a footnote, when she is cited at all.

## Recognition Slowly Catching Up With the Facts

It is not that science ignored the value of her finds: the specimens she extracted are still on display at the Natural History Museum in London, studied for two centuries. It is the person who was long erased from the act. The catch-up comes late and in fragments. In 2010, for its 350th anniversary, the Royal Society consults a panel of five women experts, four scientists and a historian of science, and ranks Anning among the ten women who most shaped the history of British science, alongside a handful of others, almost all of whom also remained for a long time on the margins of the institutions that used their work. In 2015, one hundred sixty-eight years after her death, paleontologists Dean Lomax and Judy Massare redescribe an ichthyosaur specimen that had been poorly classified in a Yorkshire museum and name it *Ichthyosaurus anningae*: an entire species finally bears her name. The fossil has not changed since 1811; it is the question of who has the right to be its author that took two centuries to evolve.

repere.texte: Mary Anning dies in 1847 without ever having been able to become a Fellow of the Geological Society of London, which admits women only from May 21, 1919, seventy-two years later. In 2010, the Royal Society ranks her among the ten women who most influenced the history of British science.

carte.punch: She found the fossils; others signed the papers.
carte.idee: In the 19th century, Mary Anning unearths the first complete ichthyosaur, plesiosaur and pterosaur in Great Britain. The buyers of her fossils publish under their own names: the Geological Society of London admits women only in 1919, 72 years after her death.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Mary Anning: The unsung hero of fossil discovery - Natural History Museum
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Detail of Anning's main discoveries and of the social context of Lyme Regis in the early 19th century.

quiz.question: Why did Mary Anning never publish the discoveries she made herself?
choix: Because she could not correctly identify the fossils she found
Because women could not become members of the Geological Society of London before 1919
Because she refused to collaborate with the scientists of her time
Because none of her fossils was complete enough to be published
quiz.explication: The Geological Society admits women as Fellows only from 1919. Anning did, however, correctly identify her fossils, some of her buyers were more mistaken than she was, and several of her finds, far from being incomplete, are now displayed whole at the Natural History Museum.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the first major discovery attributed to Mary Anning, uncovered in November 1812?
choix: The first complete plesiosaur skeleton ever unearthed, in December 1823
The skeleton of an ichthyosaur more than five meters long, the first identified as such
The first British pterosaur ever discovered, a Dimorphodon, in 1828
A nest of fossilized eggs attributed to a previously unknown theropod dinosaur
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In November 1812, Mary Anning uncovers the rest of a marine skeleton more than five meters long, the first ichthyosaur ever identified as such, after her brother Joseph had spotted its skull in 1811.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Royal Society do in 2010, for the 350th anniversary of its founding, regarding Mary Anning?
choix: It posthumously grants her the Fellow status that had been denied her in her lifetime
It funds the restoration of her birthplace in Lyme Regis
It ranks her, through a panel of five women experts, among the ten women who most shaped the history of British science
It republishes under her own name the articles describing her discoveries
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 2010, a panel of five women experts convened by the Royal Society ranks Anning among the ten women who most shaped the history of British science, for the society's 350th anniversary.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens in 2015, one hundred sixty-eight years after Mary Anning's death?
choix: A British court posthumously restores to her the copyright on her discoveries
The Natural History Museum removes from its collections the fossils she had sold
The Geological Society posthumously grants her Fellow status
Paleontologists redescribe an ichthyosaur specimen and name it Ichthyosaurus anningae in her honor
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 2015, Dean Lomax and Judy Massare redescribe a poorly classified ichthyosaur specimen and name it Ichthyosaurus anningae: an entire species finally bears Mary Anning's name.
